chapters.title: Narrative Resumed by Jim Hawkins: The Garrison in the Stockade
paragraphs: The moment Ben Gunn caught sight of the colours, he stopped short, gripped my arm, and sat down.
“There,” he said. “Those are your friends, no mistake.”
“Far likelier it's the mutineers,” I said.

“Them?” he cried. “Why, in a spot like this, where nobody puts in but gentlemen of fortune, Silver would fly the Jolly Roger — you can be sure of that. No, those are your friends. There's been fighting, too, and I reckon your friends have had the better of it; and here they are ashore in the old stockade that Flint built years and years ago. Ah, Flint had a head on him, he did! Rum aside, there was never his match. Afraid of nobody, he wasn't — nobody but Silver. Silver was that genteel.”
“Well,” said I, “maybe that's how it is. All the more reason for me to hurry on and join them.”

“Not you, mate,” said Ben. “You're a good lad, or I'm much mistaken — but you're only a lad, when all's said. Now, Ben Gunn's a sharp one. Rum itself wouldn't carry me where you're headed — not rum — not till I've seen your born gentleman and have his word of honour. And don't forget what I told you: ‘A precious sight' — that's what you'll say — ‘a precious sight more confidence' — and then you nip him.”
And he pinched me a third time with the same knowing look.

“And when Ben Gunn's wanted, you know where to find him, Jim. Right where you found him today. And the one who comes must carry something white in his hand, and he must come alone. Oh — and you'll tell him this: ‘Ben Gunn,' says you, ‘has reasons of his own.'”
“Well,” said I, “I think I follow. You've a proposal to make, you want to see the squire or the doctor, and you're to be found where I found you. Is that the whole of it?”
“And when? says you,” he added. “Why, from about noon till around six bells.”
“Good,” said I. “Now may I go?”

“You won't forget?” he asked anxiously. “Precious sight, and reasons of his own, says you. Reasons of his own — that's the mainstay, as between man and man. Well then” — still holding on to me — “I reckon you can go, Jim. And Jim — if you was to run across Silver, you wouldn't go and sell out Ben Gunn? Wild horses wouldn't drag it out of you? No, says you. And if those pirates camp ashore, Jim — well, what would you say to there being widows by morning?”

Here he was cut off by a loud report, and a cannonball came tearing through the trees and buried itself in the sand not a hundred yards from where the two of us stood talking. The next instant we had each bolted in opposite directions.

For a good hour afterward the island shook with repeated reports, and balls kept crashing through the woods. I went from one hiding place to the next, forever pursued — or so it felt — by those terrifying missiles. But toward the end of the bombardment, though I still dared not head toward the stockade, where the balls fell thickest, I had begun to take heart a little, and after a long loop to the east I crept down among the trees along the shore.

The sun had just gone down, the sea breeze was rustling and tumbling through the woods and ruffling the grey surface of the anchorage; the tide was far out as well, and broad stretches of sand lay bare. After the heat of the day, the air chilled me through my jacket.

The Hispaniola still lay at her anchorage — but sure enough, the Jolly Roger, the black flag of piracy, now flew from her peak. Even as I watched, another red flash and report sent the echoes clattering, and one more round-shot whistled overhead. That was the last of the cannonade.

I lay a while watching the activity that followed the attack. Down on the beach near the stockade, men were hacking something to pieces with axes — the poor jolly-boat, I learned later. Off near the river mouth a great fire glowed among the trees, and one of the gigs kept shuttling between that point and the ship, the men — so grim before — now shouting at the oars like children. But there was a note in their voices that smelled of rum.

At last I judged I might start back toward the stockade. I was well down the low, sandy spit that closes the anchorage to the east and joins Skeleton Island at half-tide; and as I got to my feet, I saw, some way further along the spit, an isolated rock rising from the low bushes — fairly tall, and oddly white. It struck me this might be the white rock Ben Gunn had mentioned, and that one day a boat might be wanted and I would know where to look for one.
Then I worked my way through the woods until I had come round to the back — the shoreward side — of the stockade, and was soon given a warm welcome by the faithful party.

I quickly told my story and began to take stock of my surroundings. The log-house was built of unsquared pine trunks — roof, walls, and floor alike. The floor stood in places a foot or a foot and a half above the sand. There was a porch at the door, and under it the little spring welled up into an odd sort of basin — nothing but a great iron ship's kettle with its bottom knocked out, sunk ‘to her bearings,' as the captain put it, in the sand.
Little was left of the house but its frame, though in one corner a stone slab had been laid down for a hearth, and an old rusty iron basket stood ready to hold the fire.

The slopes of the knoll and the whole inside of the stockade had been stripped of timber to build the house, and the stumps showed what a fine, tall grove had been cut down. Most of the soil had washed away or buried itself in drift once the trees were gone; only where the stream ran down from the kettle did a thick bed of moss, with some ferns and little creeping bushes, stay green among the sand. Close around the stockade — too close for defence, the others said — the wood still grew tall and dense: all fir on the land side, but toward the sea mixed heavily with live-oaks.

The cold evening breeze I mentioned whistled through every chink of the rough building and sprinkled the floor with a steady fall of fine sand. There was sand in our eyes, sand in our teeth, sand in our supper, sand dancing in the spring at the bottom of the kettle for all the world like porridge coming to a boil. Our chimney was a square hole in the roof; only a little of the smoke found its way out, and the rest swirled about the house and kept us coughing and wiping our streaming eyes.

Add to all this that Gray, the new man, had his face tied up in a bandage over a cut he'd taken breaking away from the mutineers, and that poor old Tom Redruth, still unburied, lay stiff and stark along the wall under the Union Jack.

Had we been left to sit idle, we'd all have sunk into gloom, but Captain Smollett was never one for that. He called us all up before him and split us into watches: the doctor, Gray, and I on one; the squire, Hunter, and Joyce on the other. Tired as we were, two were sent out for firewood, two more set to dig Redruth's grave; the doctor was named cook, I was posted sentry at the door, and the captain went from man to man, keeping our spirits up and lending a hand wherever it was wanted.
Every so often the doctor stepped to the door for a breath of air and to rest his eyes, which were all but smoked out of his head; and each time he did, he'd a word for me.
“Smollett,” he told me once, “is a better man than I am — and coming from me, Jim, that's saying plenty.”
Another time he came and stood silent a while. Then he cocked his head and looked at me.
“Is this Ben Gunn a man?” he asked.
“I don't know, sir,” said I. “I'm not quite sure he's sane.”

“If there's any doubt about it, then he is,” said the doctor. “A man who's spent three years biting his nails on a desert island, Jim, can't be expected to seem as sane as you or me. It isn't in human nature. Cheese, you said — that was what he craved?”
“Yes, sir — cheese,” I answered.

“Well, Jim,” says he, “see now the good of being particular about your food. You've noticed my snuff-box? And you've never once seen me take snuff — the reason being that what I carry in it is a piece of Parmesan, a very nourishing cheese made in Italy. Well — that's for Ben Gunn!”

Before supper we buried old Tom in the sand and stood round him a while, bare-headed in the breeze. A fair amount of firewood had been brought in, but not enough to please the captain, who shook his head over it and told us we ‘must get back to this tomorrow a deal livelier.' Then, when we'd eaten our pork and each had a stiff glass of brandy grog, the three chiefs drew together in a corner to talk over our chances.

It seems they were at their wits' end. The stores were so low that we'd have been starved into surrender long before any help could arrive. Our best hope, they decided, was to pick off the buccaneers until they either struck their flag or made off with the Hispaniola. From nineteen they were already down to fifteen; two more were wounded, and one at least — the man shot beside the gun — badly, if he wasn't dead. Every time we got a clear shot at them we were to take it, while guarding our own lives with the utmost care. And besides that, we had two solid allies: rum and the climate.

As for the first, though we lay half a mile off, we could hear them roaring and singing far into the night; and as for the second, the doctor staked his wig that, camped where they were in the marsh and with no medicines, half of them would be flat on their backs within the week.
“So,” he added, “if we're not all shot down first, they'll be glad enough to clear out in the schooner. It's a ship, after all, and they can take up buccaneering again, I suppose.”
“The first ship I ever lost,” said Captain Smollett.
I was dead tired, as you can imagine; and when at last I dropped off — which wasn't until I'd tossed about a great deal — I slept like a log.
The others had long been up, had breakfasted, and had added half as much again to the woodpile by the time I was woken by a bustle and the sound of voices.
“A flag of truce!” I heard a voice call; and then, hard on it, an astonished cry — “Silver himself!”
At that I sprang up, rubbed my eyes, and ran to a loophole in the wall.

chapters.title: Silver's Embassy
paragraphs: Sure enough, there were two men just beyond the stockade — one of them waving a white cloth, the other none other than Silver, standing calmly by.

It was still quite early, and the coldest morning I think I was ever out in — a chill that bored into the marrow. Overhead the sky was bright and cloudless, and the treetops glowed rosy in the sun. But where Silver stood with his lieutenant everything lay in shadow, and the two of them waded knee-deep in a low white vapour that had crept up overnight out of the swamp. The chill and the mist together told a sorry tale of the island: plainly a damp, feverish, unhealthy place.
“Keep inside, men,” said the captain. “Odds are this is a trick.”
Then he hailed the buccaneer.
“Who goes there? Stand, or we fire.”
“Flag of truce,” cried Silver.

The captain stood in the porch, keeping himself well clear of any treacherous shot. He turned and spoke to us: “Doctor's watch to the lookout. Dr. Livesey, take the north side, if you please; Jim, the east; Gray, the west. The watch below, all hands load muskets. Lively, men — and careful.”
Then he turned back to the mutineers.
“And what's your flag of truce for?” he called.
This time it was the other man who answered.
“Cap'n Silver, sir — come to make terms,” he shouted.
“Cap'n Silver? Don't know him. Who's he?” cried the captain. And we heard him mutter to himself, “Captain, is it? My heart — here's a promotion!”

Long John answered for himself. “Me, sir. These poor lads chose me captain after you deserted them, sir” — leaning hard on the word ‘deserted.' “We're willing to come to terms and have done with it, fair and square. All I ask is your word, Cap'n Smollett, to let me out of this stockade safe and sound, and one minute's grace to get out of range before a shot's fired.”
“My man,” said Captain Smollett, “I haven't the slightest wish to talk to you. If you want to talk to me, come ahead — that's all. Any treachery, it'll be on your side, and the Lord help you.”
“That's enough, Cap'n,” Long John called back cheerily. “One word from you's plenty. I know a gentleman when I see one, you may lay to that.”

We could see the man with the flag of truce trying to hold Silver back — small wonder, after so cool an answer from the captain. But Silver only laughed in his face and clapped him on the back, as if the very notion of danger were absurd. Then he came up to the stockade, tossed his crutch over, got a leg across, and with great strength and skill hauled himself over the fence and dropped safely down the other side.

I'll admit I was far too caught up in all this to be the least use as a sentry; in fact I had already abandoned my eastern loophole and crept up behind the captain, who had now settled himself on the threshold, elbows on knees, head in his hands, eyes fixed on the water bubbling up out of the old iron kettle in the sand. He was whistling “Come, Lasses and Lads.”

Silver had a terrible hard time getting up the knoll. What with the steep slope, the thick stumps, and the soft sand, he and his crutch were as helpless as a ship caught in stays. But he stuck at it without a word, like a man, and at last stood before the captain and saluted him in the handsomest style. He was got up in his best — a huge blue coat thick with brass buttons hanging to his knees, and a fine laced hat shoved back on his head.
“Here you are, my man,” said the captain, lifting his head. “You'd best sit down.”
“You ain't going to let me inside, Cap'n?” complained Long John. “It's a main cold morning, sir, to be sitting out here on the sand.”

“Why, Silver,” said the captain, “if you'd chosen to be an honest man, you might be sitting in your galley now. It's your own doing. You're either my ship's cook — and then you were treated handsomely — or you're Cap'n Silver, a common mutineer and pirate, and then you can go hang!”

“Well, well, Cap'n,” said the sea-cook, sitting down on the sand as he'd been told, “you'll just have to give me a hand up again afterward, that's all. A sweet pretty place you've got here. Ah — there's Jim! Top of the morning to you, Jim. Doctor, my service to you. Why, here you all are together like one happy family, in a manner of speaking.”
“If you've something to say, my man, you'd best say it,” said the captain.

“Right you are, Cap'n Smollett,” Silver replied. “Duty's duty, to be sure. Well now — that was a neat piece of work of yours last night. I'll not deny it: a neat piece of work. Some of you handy enough with the butt-end of a handspike. And I'll not deny some of my people were shaken — maybe all of them — maybe I was shaken myself; maybe that's why I'm here for terms. But mark me, Cap'n: it won't go twice, by thunder! We'll keep a sentry posted and ease off a point on the rum. Maybe you reckon we were all three sheets to the wind. Well, I'll tell you, I was sober — only dog-tired; and had I woken a second sooner I'd have caught you at it, I would. He weren't dead when I got to him, not him.”
“Well?” says Captain Smollett, cool as you please.

Everything Silver said was a riddle to him, but you'd never have known it from his voice. As for me, I was beginning to catch on. Ben Gunn's last words came back to me. I guessed he must have paid the buccaneers a visit while they lay drunk together round their fire, and I reckoned with glee that we now had only fourteen enemies to face.
“Here it is, then,” said Silver. “We want that treasure, and we'll have it — that's our side of it. You'd as soon keep your lives, I reckon — and that's yours. You've a chart, haven't you?”
“That's as may be,” the captain answered.

“Oh, you have, I know it,” said Long John. “No call to be so short with a man; there's not a ha'porth of good in it, you may lay to that. What I mean is, we want your chart. Now, I never meant you any harm myself.”
“None of that with me, my man,” the captain cut in. “We know exactly what you meant to do, and we don't care — because now, you see, you can't do it.”
And the captain looked at him coolly and set about filling a pipe.
“If Abe Gray—” Silver burst out.

“Belay there!” cried Mr. Smollett. “Gray told me nothing, and I asked him nothing; and what's more, I'd sooner see you and him and this whole island blown sky-high into blazes first. So there's my mind for you, my man, and you can chew on it.”
This little flash of temper seemed to cool Silver off. He'd been getting nettled, but now he gathered himself.
“Like enough,” said he. “I'll set no limits on what gentlemen may or mayn't think shipshape. And seeing as you're about to take a pipe, Cap'n, I'll make so bold as do the same.”
He filled a pipe and lit it, and the two men sat smoking in silence a good while — now eyeing each other, now tamping the tobacco, now leaning forward to spit. It was as good as a play to watch them.

“Now,” Silver went on, “here it is. You hand over the chart to get the treasure by, and you quit shooting poor seamen and staving in their heads while they sleep. Do that, and we'll give you a choice. Either you come aboard with us once the treasure's stowed, and I'll give you my affidavy, on my word of honour, to set you down somewhere safe ashore. Or, if that don't suit — some of my hands being rough, with old scores to settle over the hazing — then you can bide here. We'll share out the stores with you, man for man, and I'll give my affidavy, same as before, to hail the first ship I sight and send her back to take you off. Now there's talking for you. Handsomer than that you couldn't hope to get, not you. And I hope” — lifting his voice — “that every man in this here block house will weigh my words, for what's said to one is said to all.”
Captain Smollett rose and knocked the ashes out of his pipe into the palm of his left hand.
“Is that all?” he asked.
“Every last word, by thunder!” answered John. “Turn that down, and the next you'll see of me is musket-balls.”

“Very good,” said the captain. “Now hear me. Come up one at a time, unarmed, and I'll undertake to clap you all in irons and carry you home to a fair trial in England. Refuse, and — my name's Alexander Smollett, I've flown my sovereign's colours, and I'll see the lot of you down to Davy Jones. You can't find the treasure. You can't sail the ship — there's not a man among you fit to. You can't fight us — Gray there got clear of five of you. Your ship's in irons, Master Silver; you're on a lee shore, and so you'll find. I stand here and tell you so, and these are the last kind words you'll get from me, for by heaven I'll put a ball in your back the next time we meet. Now march, my lad. Out of this, and quick about it — hand over hand, on the double.”
Silver's face was a sight; his eyes started from his head with fury. He shook the fire out of his pipe.
“Give me a hand up!” he cried.
“Not I,” returned the captain.
“Who'll give me a hand up?” he roared.
Not one of us stirred. Snarling the vilest curses, he dragged himself along the sand until he reached the porch and could haul himself back onto his crutch. Then he spat into the spring.

“There!” he cried. “That's what I think of the lot of you. Inside the hour I'll stave in your old block house like a rum cask. Laugh away, by thunder — laugh! Inside the hour you'll be laughing the other side of your faces. The ones that die will be the lucky ones.”

And with a hideous oath he stumped off, floundering through the sand, was hauled over the stockade — after four or five tries — by the man with the flag of truce, and vanished among the trees an instant later.

chapters.title: The Attack
paragraphs: The moment Silver was gone, the captain, who had been watching him closely, turned back into the house and found not a man of us at his post but Gray. It was the first time we'd ever seen him angry.

“Quarters!” he roared. And as we all slunk back to our places: “Gray,” he said, “I'll put your name in the log; you stood by your duty like a seaman. Mr. Trelawney, I'm surprised at you, sir. Doctor — I thought you'd worn the king's coat! If that's how you served at Fontenoy, sir, you'd have done better to stay in your berth.”
The doctor's watch were all back at their loopholes, the rest busy loading the spare muskets, and every man red in the face, you may be sure, and with a flea in his ear, as the saying goes.
A while the captain watched in silence. Then he spoke.

“My lads,” said he, “I gave Silver a broadside. I poured it in red-hot on purpose; and before the hour's out, just as he said, we'll be boarded. We're outnumbered — I needn't tell you that — but we fight under cover; and a minute ago I'd have said we fought with discipline. I've no doubt at all we can beat them off, if you choose to.”
Then he made his rounds and saw, as he put it, that all was clear.

On the two short sides of the house, east and west, there were only two loopholes; on the south side, where the porch stood, two more; and on the north side, five. We had a round twenty muskets for the seven of us. The firewood had been stacked into four piles — tables, you might call them — one toward the middle of each wall, and on each lay some ammunition and four loaded muskets, ready to the defenders' hands. In the middle, the cutlasses were laid out in a row.
“Douse the fire,” said the captain. “The chill's past, and we can't have smoke in our eyes.”
Mr. Trelawney carried the whole iron fire-basket out bodily, and smothered the embers in sand.

“Hawkins hasn't had his breakfast. Hawkins, help yourself and take it back to your post,” the captain went on. “Lively, lad — you'll want it before you're through. Hunter, serve out a round of brandy to all hands.”
And while this went on, the captain finished working out, in his own mind, the plan of defence.

“Doctor, you'll take the door,” he resumed. “Mind you don't expose yourself; keep inside and fire through the porch. Hunter, the east side, there. Joyce, you stand by the west, my man. Mr. Trelawney, you're the best shot — you and Gray take this long north wall with its five loopholes; that's where the danger lies. If they can reach it and fire in on us through our own ports, things will turn ugly. Hawkins, neither you nor I count for much at the shooting; we'll stand by to load and lend a hand.”

As the captain had said, the chill was past. The moment the sun cleared our girdle of trees, it came down full force on the clearing and drank up the vapours at one draught. Soon the sand was baking and the resin sweating out of the logs of the block house. Jackets and coats were thrown off, shirts opened at the neck and rolled to the shoulder; and there we stood, each at his post, in a fever of heat and suspense.
An hour went by.
“Hang them!” said the captain. “Dull as the doldrums, this. Gray — whistle us up a wind.”
And just then came the first sign of the attack.
“Begging your pardon, sir,” said Joyce, “am I to fire if I see anyone?”
“I told you so!” cried the captain.
“Thank you, sir,” said Joyce, with the same quiet courtesy.

Nothing came of it for a time, but the question had put us all on edge, ears and eyes straining — the musketeers with their pieces balanced in their hands, the captain out in the middle of the block house, mouth set tight and a frown on his face.

So a few seconds passed, until all at once Joyce threw up his musket and fired. The report had hardly died when it was answered, again and again, by a scattering volley from outside — shot after shot, like a string of geese, from every side of the enclosure. Several bullets struck the log-house, but not one came through; and as the smoke thinned and cleared, the stockade and the woods around it looked as still and empty as before. Not a branch stirred, not the gleam of a barrel betrayed our enemies.
“Did you hit your man?” asked the captain.
“No, sir,” Joyce answered. “I believe not, sir.”
“Next best thing's to tell the truth,” muttered Captain Smollett. “Load his gun, Hawkins. How many on your side would you say there were, doctor?”
“I know exactly,” said Dr. Livesey. “Three shots from this side. I saw the three flashes — two close together, one further west.”
“Three!” the captain repeated. “And how many on yours, Mr. Trelawney?”

But that wasn't so easily answered. Many had come from the north — seven by the squire's count, eight or nine by Gray's. From east and west only a single shot each. Plainly, then, the real attack would come from the north, and on the other three sides we'd only be harried by a show of force. Still, Captain Smollett made no change in his arrangements. If the mutineers got over the stockade, he argued, they'd seize any unguarded loophole and shoot us down like rats in our own stronghold.

Nor had we much time left for thinking. Suddenly, with a loud hurrah, a little knot of pirates burst from the woods on the north side and rushed straight at the stockade. At the same instant fire opened again from the trees, and a rifle ball came singing through the doorway and smashed the doctor's musket to bits.

The boarders swarmed over the fence like monkeys. Squire and Gray fired again and again; three men dropped, one pitching forward into the enclosure, two falling back outside. But one of those was more frightened than hurt, for he was on his feet in a flash and gone among the trees.

Two were down for good, one had fled, and four had got a footing inside our defences, while from the cover of the woods seven or eight men, each plainly carrying several muskets, kept up a hot but useless fire on the log-house.

The four who had boarded made straight for the building, shouting as they came, and the men in the trees shouted back to cheer them on. Several shots were fired, but in their haste not one of the marksmen seems to have hit a thing. In a moment the four pirates had scrambled up the mound and were on us.
Job Anderson, the boatswain, showed his head at the middle loophole.
“At 'em, all hands — all hands!” he roared in a voice of thunder.

At the same moment another pirate seized Hunter's musket by the muzzle, wrenched it out of his hands, dragged it through the loophole, and with one stunning blow laid the poor fellow senseless on the floor. Meanwhile a third, running clear round the house unharmed, appeared all at once in the doorway and fell with his cutlass on the doctor.
Our whole position was reversed. A moment before we'd been firing, under cover, on an exposed enemy; now it was we who stood exposed and could not strike a blow in return.
The log-house was thick with smoke, and to that we owed our relative safety. Cries and confusion, the flashes and cracks of pistol-shots, and one loud groan rang in my ears.
“Out you go, lads — out and at them in the open! Cutlasses!” cried the captain.

I snatched a cutlass from the pile, and someone else, grabbing another at the same moment, gave me a cut across the knuckles that I scarcely felt. I dashed out the door into the bright sun. Someone was close at my heels, I didn't know who. Straight ahead, the doctor was driving his man down the hill, and just as my eyes fell on him he beat down the fellow's guard and sent him sprawling on his back with a great slash across the face.
“Round the house, lads — round the house!” cried the captain; and even through the din I caught the change in his voice.

Without thinking, I obeyed, turned east, and with my cutlass up ran round the corner of the house. The next moment I was face to face with Anderson. He gave a roar, and his hanger went up over his head, flashing in the sun. I had no time to be afraid, but as the blow still hung above me I sprang aside, missed my footing in the soft sand, and rolled headlong down the slope.

When I'd first burst from the door, the other mutineers had already been swarming up the palisade to finish us. One man, in a red night-cap, his cutlass between his teeth, had even got astride the top. Yet so short was the interval that when I found my feet again everything stood just as before — the fellow in the red night-cap still half over, another just showing his head above the stockade. And yet, in that single breath, the fight was over and the day was ours.

Gray, hard behind me, had cut down the big boatswain before he could recover from his last stroke. Another had been shot at a loophole in the very act of firing into the house, and now lay dying, the pistol still smoking in his hand. A third, as I'd seen, the doctor had dropped with one blow. Of the four who'd scaled the palisade, only one was left unaccounted for, and he — having dropped his cutlass on the field — was now scrambling back out with the fear of death on him.
“Fire — fire from the house!” cried the doctor. “And you, lads, back under cover.”

But no one heeded him; not a shot was fired, and the last boarder got clean away and vanished with the rest into the wood. In three seconds nothing was left of the attacking party but the five who had fallen — four inside the palisade and one without.
The doctor, Gray, and I ran for shelter at full speed. The survivors would soon be back where they'd left their muskets, and the firing might start up again at any moment.

By now the house was somewhat clear of smoke, and at a glance we saw the price of our victory. Hunter lay stunned beside his loophole; Joyce, by his, shot through the head, never to stir again; while right in the centre the squire was holding up the captain, the one as pale as the other.
“The captain's wounded,” said Mr. Trelawney.
“Have they run?” asked Mr. Smollett.
“Every man that could, you may be sure,” the doctor answered; “but there's five of them that'll never run again.”

“Five!” cried the captain. “Come, that's better. Five against three leaves us four to nine. That's better odds than we started with. Seven to nineteen we were then — or thought we were — and that's as hard to bear.” *

*The mutineers were soon down to only eight, for the man Mr. Trelawney had shot aboard the schooner died of his wound that same evening. But of course the faithful party did not learn this until later.
